projects.title: Show HN: AI agent needs process to build a commercial application
projects.author: abalgir
projects.summary: I decided to test this claim with my app, NoMoreHappyPath (NMHP), against Claude on a real project. Here is the test: I built Acremuse, a commercial real estate analysis platform, with Claude Desktop and Codex as a reviewer. It is deployed and used today by a couple of investors. Then I wondered what I'd missed that might bite me later. ~ 374,000 Lines of program code - 1,070 Source files (Python and TypeScript) - ~ 11,400 Functions and methods - 3,067 Automated tests So I gave the same 374k-line code snapshot and the same brief to one Claude session that can use Codex as a reviewer and to my own tool, NMHP. My directive was the same for both: Analyze the code, find any errors/bugs, and list them by severity. Findings must be reviewed before writing the final report. The Results (Verified by an impartial, blind Codex judge): NMHP: 33 real issues found. 7 false claims. Claude: 10 real issues found. 2 false claims. Only 6 issues overlapped. Time & Cost: From the owner's go-ahead to the reviewer's pass, NoMoreHappyPath took about 74 minutes, including time lost while it found and worked around a defect in the product itself. The Python version NMHP was working on was 3.9, the OS version, and it didn't have pytest installed, which was needed to verify some claims. After 15 minutes of blockage, the CTO stepped in and told the agent to create a venv with Python 3.13, install the corresponding pytest, and move the project along. NMHP CTO reacts when 15 minutes pass without movement from agents. To be fair to Claude, Claude did create a venv from the get-go. Time & Cost: NMHP took 74 minutes and cost $24 in API spend. Claude finished in a few minutes for a fraction of that cost. And yes, NMHP takes over an hour and costs twenty-four bucks. But for a 374k-line codebase, finding 23 more real issues overall that vanilla Claude missed makes $24 a massive win compared to human audit rates. I know this isn't a benchmark; it's one app and one run each. I wrote a detailed white paper on it. But it confirmed my idea: an AI agent without a real process is not yet capable of building a commercially ready application, even with a frontier model and reviews that are initiated by the same agent.

projects.title: Show HN: I built a tool that finds reliability bugs in your code
projects.author: aray07
projects.summary: Hey HN, I’m Abhishek. I'm building Opslane, a tool that finds reliability issues in your code. On every PR, it spins up your entire app and then tries to find weak spots that would break in production. Demo: https://youtu.be/47phxkdh6f0 Example: We tested Opslane on Lago (open-source billing) and found a bug where customers get double charged. Opslane made Stripe take the money and then return a 500. Lago marked the payment failed. A retry from the dashboard charged the customer again. https://github.com/getlago/lago-api/issues/6903 Why I built this I used to work on reliability at Robinhood. We used to run chaos testing in our staging environments: inject faults in various parts of the system and see what breaks. We found issues like Kafka or Redis being unavailable for a few seconds could take the whole app down. But that kind of testing was expensive. It needed a well maintained staging environment. Engineers needed to know what to test. Most teams never actually did it. Over the last year, coding agents have gone writing some of my code to almost all my code now. Teams are shipping way more code than they were 6 months ago. Code review tools read the diff, but a lot of reliability bugs aren't in the diff. They're in how your code behaves when Stripe, Redis or the network misbehaves. And e2e tests usually mock those services out and test the happy path. Agents have made this type of testing a lot cheaper. And we will see more of this (kinda like security scanning / testing) How it works A full copy of your app per PR: Postgres, Redis, Kafka, SQS, S3. Working copies of your third-party dependencies: Stripe, Slack, Gmail and more. Traffic goes through our proxy, which lets us inject failures. The agent picks what to test: It reads every PR and writes down invariants that need to hold (for e.g. a customer should never be charged twice). It then injects faults likely to break the invariants. Bugs we've found We ran Opslane on some popular open-source apps and here are some of the bugs we have found: 1/ Twenty: deleting a workspace while Stripe is failing locks everyone out, and billing keeps going. Twenty merged a fix. ( https://github.com/twentyhq/twenty/issues/28043 ) 2/ Dub: a restart in the middle of a payout paid a partner $240 for $120 owed. ( https://github.com/dubinc/dub.link/issues/4707 ) Full list: opslane.com/open-source Opslane is pretty early - we have a couple of early customers. We have found bugs in their system that their other code review tools missed. Would love to get feedback from folks and how they are seeing the reliability of their systems evolve over time with agents.

projects.title: 【开源自荐】ClinicalFaultBench：度量临床 AI 智能体"怎么失败"的失效审计基准
projects.author: hongjunt50-afk

github.name: hongjunt50-afk/ClinicalFaultBench
github.description: 面向医疗 AI 智能体的失效审计基准:在坏数据、坏工具、坏时序下,度量临床大模型智能体的失败方式、错误传播与不确定性表达。主实验用 Synthea 纯合成患者,零合规风险、可公开复现。

projects.summary: ClinicalFaultBench 是一个面向临床 AI 智能体的失效审计基准,MIT 开源。 现在几乎所有医疗 AI 评测都在"理想输入"下算成功率。但这个方向有个被绕开的问题:真实医院的检验单会缺项、单位会错、报告是几天前的、系统会截断返回结果。agent 在这些情况下怎么崩,没人系统测过。 于是这个项目做的事很简单——往 agent 的环境里注入"看起来合理但错"的临床故障,然后量它怎么失败: 七类故障:关键化验缺失 / 单位错误(mg/dL 与 SI 制错位)/ 矛盾记录 / 陈旧数据(时间戳前移)/ 结果截断 / 跨患者污染 / 时间线漂移,每类两档严重度 五项指标:注入前后配对错误率、错误传播率、患者安全违规率、不确定性校准、自纠率 三类任务:入院摘要审查 / 医嘱冲突审查 / 出院准备 有意思的发现 最有价值的一条是负结果:结果截断让两个模型分别掉 0.389 / 0.365,而"截 30%"与"截 70%"的伤害逐位相等——缺多少不重要,有没有意识到缺了才重要。模型从不确认数据是否完整。 另一条:禁忌冲突检测已经饱和(检出率约 100%,效应约 0),如实写进报告了。 更值得分享的教训 这个项目第一版出了七条结论,其中五条后来被证明是判分器 bug 造成的伪影,而且每条都错得毫无报错。最阴的一个:参考区间只按 LOINC 码查、没看单位,同一码不同单位量纲差 40 倍,导致 100% 的 fL 制 RDW 被判成异常,一路污染了答案键。 现在这七个坑全部固化成 23 个回归测试。 特点 主实验用纯合成 Synthea 患者(Apache-2.0),仓库里零受限数据,克隆下来不花钱就能跑完纯规则部分(不需要任何 API key) 中文文档为主 代码结构对"数据不出院"的场景留了接口:代码进医院跑,只回传聚合指标

projects.summary: I’ve spent the last year building context for AI analysts in the mid-market. I’ve open sourced a library from my learnings, along the same principles of the Matt Pocock skills. Principles: * Claude / Codex / Cursor etc are great data agents - you just need context to enable them to answer business questions correctly. * Much of the important context lives in analysts heads' * Context must be maintainable (short, human readable - markdown and yaml) * Added context should be load bearing, not repeat of information that is available in another source of truth - and evaluations prove the value of the context * Companies should own their own context, and must be shareable with any model * Context should be version controlled (and github works as a context store). What the library does: * Performs an interview with your analysts (context-interview skill), one domain at a time, similar to what I have done as a consultant. The interview is informed by your query logs. * The AI develops evaluation questions at the same time as building the context - and at the end of each domain interview asks you to run an evaluation with and without the context. The evaluation will actually check the results against your dashboards if you allow it. We have shown increases in accuracy from 87% to 95% by adding this context in our imaginary open-source company, Shorelane. * Provides a set of skills to use the context that follow best practices for self service analytics: * Write a plain english plan for the business user to approve * Execute the plan * Verify that the execution followed the plan, and provide a simple uncertainty score. * Enable a adversarial review of the answer if their are doubts. What you get: Context repo written in markdown and yaml after you finish the interview. We use a single github repo, divided into domains. The interview can be shared and restarted by checking in/out of github. A set of skills to share with your business team Optional: We offer a fast MCP server to serve the Github-based context to your team.

projects.title: Show HN: Markdown is 40× more token-efficient with SQLite
projects.author: richardcrng
projects.summary: Hi HN, I'm Richard, founder of Native. I'm working on open-source context ownership, to stop AI centralisation: https://github.com/withnative/native My first focus has been making Markdown vaults powerful enough so that teams can self-host all of their context (messaging, docs and projects), without it being externally fragmented or rate-limited. I'm sharing some early results: Markdown vaults can be 40× more efficient with SQLite! https://www.withnative.ai/research-and-posts/markdown-contex... Here's some of the main ideas: - SQLite or Markdown folders, you pick. You can project the same authoritative event log into either form; more projection formats will follow (e.g. maybe neo4j; we do use a graph structure). - Empirically: SQLite is better for agents! On a 120 trial evaluation for 11,000 records, agents use 40× fewer tokens with SQLite vs Markdown, per correct answer. - Everything is a file or SQLite row. Messages, documents and projects: all can be modelled in your vault. You get local-first collaboration with teammates, synced to a cloud of your choice. - You can render your vault with arbitrary UI. Your WhatsApp-like UI speaks to your teammate's Slack-like UI; both are just views over the same database. A few things I've learned building this: - Agents do pretty well even without SQL if you give them strongly typed Markdown frontmatter. This was one arm of the trial I ran. I didn't have any clear expectations, but it was cool to watch: agents ended up writing Python scripts to do SQL-like queries. - Cumulatively, cached input tokens can get expensive. I feel silly in hindsight here. I'd gotten used to letting my sessions run long, "It's all cached so it's very cheap". But when I looked at my results here, over 2/3 of the token bill on long sessions was cached input... - "Markdown vaults don't scale as well as databases" isn't as self-evident as I think. This is why I decided to benchmark it... I've had some very blank stares when I try to explain how Markdown files might break at true agent-scale volume. Unfortunately, the dataset is private, because it's two months of my own work. I am considering open-sourcing it even so, but there is definitely some embarrassing stuff in there. TBD... I know that independent result verification matters! The core engine that I evaluated is open-source, with more to be released soon: https://github.com/withnative/native If you're interested in trying connected context on an open engine, you can get updates from our website or email me directly: richard@withnative.ai https://www.withnative.ai/

projects.author: Thneonl
projects.summary: 给 AI agent 做了个 MCP 执法网关（ Rust ），核心问题：当两个决策模型对同一件事给出不同判断时，怎么安全处理？ 实测：同一个越权场景（ coding agent 试图 merge 夹带无关变更的 PR ）： - Jev 给 0.94 置信度 → 准入层 Accept → 授权挂起 → DENY - d3 （ vLLM SR ）给 0.70 → Hold → 什么都不改 → ALLOW 两个都对。分歧不是 bug ，是校准本性（ d3 ECE 4.3 vs Jev 8.0 ）。治理层的价值在于让分歧安全。 网关做的事：每个 tools/call 先过 r2r_decide 门控，ALLOW 转发上游，DENY 返回 isError + 证据文本（相位 + 规则 + 事件 ID ），全程审计到 EventStore 。 零 API key 复现： cargo run -- fixture cargo run -- fixture --provider d3 GitHub: https://github.com/Thneoly/r2r-jev （ Apache-2.0, v0.2.0 ）

projects.title: Show HN: PatchWave - Add static analysis and automerge to Dependabot
projects.author: blimmer
projects.summary: Hey Hacker News, we're Ben, Josh, and Donnie, co-founders of PatchWave. PatchWave is a GitHub App that combines static analysis and eval'ed agents to analyze and (optionally) auto-merge PRs it deems as safe. If a Dependabot PR breaks your CI build, a fix agent works to get CI passing again. Dependabot PRs suck. Nobody likes dealing with them. Most of the time they go ignored or a senior engineer spends their valuable time dealing with them. Before PatchWave, I ran a freelance business charging clients hourly to do exactly this kind of "keep the lights on" work. Even at our small startup, we'd spend Monday mornings dealing with Dependabot PRs. Having a human-in-the-loop working with an agent on these PRs was time consuming and, often, agents would get lazy and not actually validate how an upstream change affected the codebase. And, as the quantity and severity of CVEs increases, merging security updates quickly becomes increasingly important. PatchWave is a set of specialized agents that uses static analysis tools on context we gather deterministically. 1. We pull the changelog, the code diff between versions, security advisories, and CI results. 2. The agent checks out your code in an isolated sandbox, where it uses structural code search, type checkers and your project's own toolchain to understand how your codebase uses each dependency being updated. Every Dependabot PR gets a report. You can see a few examples (against OSS repos) here: https://reports.patchwave.ai/alam00000/bentopdf/pull/913 and https://reports.patchwave.ai/shipshapecode/shepherd/pull/355... 3. If CI fails, we automatically dispatch a fix agent to try to get CI green again. For most PRs, this means updating your code to use a newer API, fixing linting/formatting issues, etc. 4. We have an optional feature that allows auto-merging certain PRs when PatchWave deems them as safe and the PR aligns with your auto-merge policy. Our recommended auto-merge policy is to auto-merge patch/minor/major dev dependencies and patch/minor production dependencies. You can customize this policy or turn auto-merge off entirely. PatchWave will skip auto-merge in a bunch of cases where a human should review. For instance, if provenance changes (e.g., a package that's usually published by GitHub Actions via Trusted Publishing is suddenly published by an API Key), we require human review before merging. Dependabot also instituted an on-by-default 3-day cooldown to reduce the risk of supply chain attacks. If PatchWave makes any changes via a fix agent, we'll always require your review before merge. Currently, PatchWave only works with Dependabot and GitHub. We plan to offer Renovate support in the future. We've eval'ed the agents the most against TypeScript and Ruby, but are always adding to our eval suite to improve accuracy. The fix agent works best with PRs that require modest code changes. For large updates, especially updates that span multiple majors, our fix agent will give up and provide you a remediation plan to help you mitigate. On the privacy/security side of the house, our SOC 2 Type II audit is in progress (see trust.contextbridge.ai). We only run on repos you select, our agents run in a short-lived microVM per run, we use Amazon Bedrock with zero-data-retention, and never train on your code. We're offering 25 free PRs per GitHub org, per month with no credit card required. Additional PRs are billed at about $1/PR, with discounts for higher volume. We also would love to accelerate OSS projects, so reach out to ask about additional free credits. If you hate dealing with Dependabot PRs, we'd love for you to give it a shot and tell us what you think. Josh, Donnie, and I will be around answering any questions and responding to any feedback you have.

projects.author: dustinkirkland
projects.summary: I'm Dustin Kirkland, author of Byobu. I recently flew to Australia and kept nudging my Claude, Codex, and Bash jobs along back home from somewhere over the Pacific, at 700ms of latency. That's what Trustmux is for: secure, asynchronous access to your tmux or Byobu sessions from your phone. I first posted this in June and since then there have been many point releases, lots of new features and testing, and a growing base of users. It's now packaged in Ubuntu 26.10, Debian, Fedora, and Chainguard OS. Why not SSH, Mosh, or Claude Mobile? - SSH/Mosh: a live, synchronous connection is brutal on a phone. Latency and WiFi-to-cellular handoffs make it laggy and fragile. - Claude Mobile: great for Claude, but I wanted access to whatever is running in my tmux session: shells, Claude, other code assistants. Trustmux is async by design. Connect, look, type a command, disconnect, with no fragile connection state to babysit. Security: TLS with real certificates, end to end. Uses Tailscale (cert provisioning via tailscale serve, no port forwarding) optionally, bind to your own network address, or bring your own or self-signed certs. Two security experts reviewed the design and I implemented their recommendations. More scrutiny is very welcome. Quick start: trustmux enable trustmux start trustmux pair # shows a QR code if qrencode is installed Open the URL on your phone, enter the 6-digit code, and add it to your home screen. It's a PWA, so there's no app store. Install: apt, dnf, pip install trustmux, or brew tap dustinkirkland/trustmux && brew install trustmux Under the hood: Python, libtmux, WebSockets, Tailscale, and no polling. The UI shell is cached for offline use. Part of Byobu, GPLv3. Trustmux isn't affiliated with the tmux project. https://trustmux.dev https://github.com/dustinkirkland/byobu https://pypi.org/project/trustmux/

projects.title: Show HN: Eevo – Consequential Decision Model
projects.author: ojalajuho
projects.summary: Hi HN, I'm Juho from Upright. I think we may have stumbled upon an interesting approach to AI alignment. The idea is as follows: 1. train a decision model to be really good at comparative sizing of consequences, expected value problems, and modelling overlap between different consequences 2. create a harness around that model that accepts a decision context, list of options, and identified consequences, then runs pairwise comparisons and overlap modelling for the consequences using the decision model in (1), and finally solves implied relative consequences "sizes" and finally EV (for different stakeholders) 3. Make AI agents running on general purpose LLMs use (2) to make better decisions. So the agent provides the context, options, and identifies the consequences, Eevo model just sizes them, models their overlap, and computes EV. In practice this seems to improve agent judgement a lot (in addition to adding lots of practical observability) It seems the (well-motivated) emphasis on instruction-following hurts model's performance on expected value tasks. The underlying decision model we trained beats Jev, Clef, MS decision-1 the model on OpenAI decisions API on economic rationality benchmarks like STEEP, expected value tasks, poker, and even Pacman (Jevman benchmark). I swear to you we did not Benchmaxx on Pacman Also it seems to be useful also for human decisions. Just getting other people's decisions presented to you in standard format with consequences listed and sized is just very pleasant. There are some testers though who think this is useful for improving everyone's judgement, except their own

projects.title: Show HN: T0: We trained a 256M SOTA open-weights time-series forecasting model
projects.author: LTMeyer

github.name: theforecastingcompany/tfc-t0
github.description: An open-weights time-series forecasting foundation model from The Forecasting Company.

projects.summary: Hi everyone, we are excited to share t0-gamma, the latest model in our t0 family. It is a 256M parameter open-weights foundation model for time series (TSFM). It runs on CPU, GPU or Apple chips. https://huggingface.co/theforecastingcompany/t0-gamma t0 leverages historical data to forecast the likely outcomes over a given horizon. It does so zero-shot. It works on almost any time series, as it can pick up small signals like trends and seasonality. It can also leverage future-known information, like holidays, promotions and weather forecasts. Under the hood, t0 is a transformer that alternates attention between time and across the variates of a series. t0 is agnostic to the domain and to the frequency of the time series. For instance, it can be used to predict retail or electricity demand, as well as server metrics. On European day ahead electricity prices, t0 reduces the error by a third compared with a naive baseline that repeats the previous day. Adding weather forecasts or holiday information improves it even further. There is a Colab notebook to try it. t0 has also been tested independently on electricity prices in Texas (ERCOT). https://colab.research.google.com/github/theforecastingcompa... Like other TSFMs, t0 outperforms classical techniques such as ARIMA, ETS and their variants. On the public benchmarks GIFT-Eval, fev-bench and TIME, t0-gamma currently ranks first among the other TSFMs. It means it is the most accurate model there is to date. Like other TSFMs, t0 can be used inside agentic, routing or ensembling systems. This can improve the scores on the leaderboards even further. Our tech report describes the model family and its evaluation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24559 Trying it takes a few Python lines. pip install "tfc-t0[torch]>=0.6.0" from t0 import T0Forecaster model = T0Forecaster.from_pretrained("theforecastingcompany/t0-gamma").eval() history = ... # history of the time series to predict out = model.predict(history, horizon=24) out.median There is more to come. We are working to extend t0 to joint forecasts across related series and hierarchies, much longer contexts and faster inference. Please give it a try, and don't hesitate to tell us where it works and where it doesn't. We are The Forecasting Company. We want to help companies reduce their uncertainty about the future, so they can make better decisions. We are starting our journey by building foundation models for time series.

projects.title: Show HN: tsv has fast formatters and parsers for Svelte, TypeScript/JS, CSS
projects.author: ryanatkn
projects.summary: tsv is a set of performance-focused language tools for the Web. Today it ships formatters and parsers for TypeScript/JS, CSS, and Svelte, including a vscode/openvsx extension. JSON and HTML are planned, maybe linting after. The readme has a loose roadmap - https://github.com/fuzdev/tsv tsv's benchmarks show how the Web's newer native tools have some performance left on the table. Formatting TypeScript, tsv is more than twice as fast as oxfmt, and is smaller and uses less memory - https://tsv.fuz.dev/docs/benchmarks From the site: - formatting TypeScript, tsv is ~2.2x faster than Oxfmt (native), ~36x faster than Prettier (native Rust vs Prettier's JS; ~26x as wasm), and ~7.6x faster than Biome (wasm) - formatting Svelte, tsv is ~79x faster than Prettier (~55x as wasm) and ~10x faster than Biome (wasm) - formatting CSS, tsv is ~3.6x faster than Oxfmt (native), ~111x faster than Prettier (~78x as wasm), and ~12x faster than Biome (wasm) tsv is focused on the Web and Svelte, and doesn't support other nonstandard languages like JSX/TSX and SCSS. This limits possible adoption, but it keeps the tool slim and simple, and there are plenty of other tools that offer a generic language platform - tsv isn't trying to compete with them. Part of my motivation was being tired of slow tools and Svelte's second-class status in this next generation. Before starting the project, I had tried to build on Oxc and Biome, and ran into some discouraging edges. On the benchmarks' language support section, you'll see Oxc doesn't export its CSS parser (recently added, a fork of Raffia - https://github.com/g-plane/raffia ), and Biome doesn't export its parsers. Also oxfmt doesn't ship wasm to the browser yet, and tsv's smaller footprint is useful there (Biome is 46.9 MB to tsv's 2.7). Parser conformance is as good or better than Oxc, Biome, and swc, except negative parser cases (errors), which are unfinished. https://tsv.fuz.dev/docs/conformance The codebase turns 1 year old at the end of the month. It's my first serious AI-generated project, built with Claude Code. I learned Rust in 2015, built some toys including an arcade action prototype, and followed its development over the years, but this is my first project since. tsv wouldn't exist without LLMs - it requires far too much labor for a side project. tsv leans heavily on Prettier, but doesn't copy it. This is why this production release took almost a year, despite the silly fast coding part. I made some different stylistic choices, more for Svelte than TypeScript, and fixed numerous quirks and bugs and documented them. tsv also takes advantage of Svelte 5's whitespace rules, which further diverged from HTML to trim leading whitespace in tags, fixing longstanding formatting warts - https://svelte.dev/docs/svelte/v5-migration-guide#Whitespace... The formatter takes no style config, and instead is hardcoded to Prettier's style with Svelte's config. Supporting Prettier's config would force significant costs on tsv with a JS runtime, so instead I'm keeping the formatters non-configurable instead of making all users pay those costs. Part of these costs can be see in the CLI benchmark (which is a fork of Oxc's official bench-formatter) - when tsv's binary is used directly instead of via Node, the single-repo CLI benchmark runs tsv 1.7x faster using less than half the memory. Next I'm exploring rearchitecting to Zig-inspired data-oriented parsing - https://mitchellh.com/zig/parser - which should get tsv closer to Yuku's speed, measured on the site. The vscode extension is `fuzdev.tsv-format` - https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=fuzdev.t... - and Open VSX - https://open-vsx.org/extension/fuzdev/tsv-format Repo: https://github.com/fuzdev/tsv

projects.title: Show HN: Hatoba, an open-source SSH client with an AI assistant and E2EE sync
projects.author: scarletkc

github.name: scarletkc/Hatoba
github.description: Open-source desktop SSH client with an AI assistant and end-to-end encrypted sync through your own Cloudflare account

projects.summary: I've used SSH tools for years and didn't really plan on building yet another SSH client, but I ended up building one the way I wanted. Hatoba is a desktop SSH client for Windows, Linux and macOS. It's written in Rust with Tauri 2 and MIT licensed. Each terminal has an AI assistant panel next to it. You describe the problem, and it reads the terminal screen, runs commands, types into the shell, and reads, edits and searches files on the host to find the cause and fix it. You can approve every command and edit it before it runs, let a model you pick approve the safe ones, or turn approval off. Files it changes show a diff you can undo. It works with any OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic API, local models included, and supports skills and MCP servers. Sync doesn't go through a server of mine. Hatoba deploys a Worker and a D1 database to your own Cloudflare account and syncs hosts, keys and AI conversations through them. The free plan usually covers personal use. Everything is encrypted on the device before it leaves. Keys are derived from your master password with Argon2id, every item is encrypted with AES-256-GCM, and the Worker only stores ciphertext plus the hashes it needs to sign you in. Someone who gets hold of the whole Cloudflare account still only gets ciphertext. Sync is optional, and everything works offline without it. The usual SSH client features are there too: groups, tags and fuzzy search, ~/.ssh/config import, ProxyJump and SOCKS5/HTTP proxies, an SFTP panel, local port forwarding, and a key vault that imports OpenSSH, PEM and PuTTY keys. There's also a dashboard showing CPU, memory, disk and network for every saved host, read over plain SSH with nothing installed on the servers. SSH is russh, the terminal is xterm.js with the WebGL renderer, and the UI is React. I develop on Windows, so it's Windows first, with a custom title bar that supports Snap Layouts and Mica, and working CJK input methods. The Linux packages and the macOS build get far less testing on real machines. The macOS build is Apple Silicon only and isn't notarized, so macOS blocks it on first launch until you allow it in Privacy & Security. Bug reports from Linux and Mac users would help the most. Website: https://hatoba.fog.moe Downloads: https://hatoba.fog.moe/download/

projects.summary: 用麦当劳官方 MCP 扫了全国 337 个地级及以上行政区的 5,817 家门店，算出一个 0~100 的城市麦当劳指数。输入城市名或地址关键词，就能看到这座城市在同级城市中的排名，以及门店密度、核心区覆盖、得来速占比三个分项。项目含纯函数计算引擎、离线数据快照与自包含演示页，打开即用、不联网。 亮点 把接口限制变成产品定义，而不是硬刚：MCP 的门店接口单次固定只返回 5 家、无分页、经纬度恒为 0.0，拿不到门店总数。项目用同构关键词采样（城市名 + 区县 + 通用道路 + 通用 POI）绕开上限，并把产品语义直接定义成「只做同级别比较」，同时在页面明写拿到的是采样下界。 一道「防假精度」护栏：给近乎无差异的指标算百分位，等于把噪声放大成排名差异。实测全国 117 个共有 SKU 的挂牌价篮子相对极差只有 0.285，低于设定的 0.30 阈值，于是价格维度被降级为「只展示、不计分」。 用公开数据反向校验自己：把采样门店数逐省与公开门店数对照，量化覆盖率，并写清偏差方向 —— 门店越密的城市越容易被低估（南京实测覆盖率仅约 59%）。 工程上可直接取用：计算引擎是纯函数、零 I/O 零第三方依赖；71 项三态自测（通过 / 失败 / 跳过，「跳过」不算通过）；演示页是单文件，打开即用，不联网也不调 MCP。

github.name: robertn702/reasoning-router
github.description: Per-step reasoning effort for coding agents, picked by a classifier, without breaking the prompt cache. OpenCode plugin, Pi extension, and a local proxy for Codex CLI.

projects.summary: 我一直把编程 Agent 的推理强度开在 high，连改名这种小事也是，用量消耗得很快。但降到 medium 又会出错：在一个较难的 pytest bug 上，GPT-6 Astra 用 medium 5 次只解决了 1 次。 所以我做了 reasoning-router。编程 Agent 每次请求模型之前，它先让一个小型分类器（默认是 TypeSafe 的 Jev，也可以换成 Cloudflare Clef、Laya 等）判断这一步需要多少推理强度，再把结果加到请求里。 切换推理强度通常会让 prompt cache 失效。它用 OpenAI 的 configurationupdate 和 Anthropic 的对话中 effort 消息来改强度，之前的上下文不变，所以缓存还能命中。 在 10 个 SWE-bench Verified 问题上，路由和固定 high 都解决了 44/44，路由少用约 14% 的输出 token，耗时少约 9%。只测了一个模型和一组任务，结果仅供参考。 支持 OpenCode 插件、Pi 扩展，以及可接入 Codex CLI 的本地代理。目前是 alpha 版本，MIT 协议。

projects.title: Show HN: Tessary – Find the AI agent failures your sampled evals miss
projects.author: infinitetrooper
projects.summary: Hey, I'm Akhil, co-founder of Tessary. An open-source agent reliability platform that monitors every production trace, detects issues that sampled evals miss, and investigates to find the root cause. We started up about a year ago building synthetic users for usability testing of B2B software, we built the agents that would personify real users and use the software but, we were never able to make them work reliably enough for long running sessions. We had built a massive eval set to tune our agents but, then the evaluation itself got prohibitively costly - like 5x costlier than actually running the agent since we needed to grade across the many narrow intents of our agent. That's where Tessary originated, we wanted to make agent reliability both cover more ground and be simultaneously less costly to run. Tessary works on 2 layers. L1 classifiers - which look at every agent trace and flag potentially erroneous ones extremely cheaply. We are talking 2-3 orders of magnitude cheaper than running the actual agent. L2 agents - which triage and find the root cause of the issue from the erroneous traces. These are run on SOTA models but, because we run them on already flagged traces, the time and $ spent finding the cause is much cheaper than running grading on even 1% of traces. In our testing on complex agents, at 1M traces, this approach was 5x cheaper than sampled evaluations and as your agent gets more reliable, the cost of reliability also goes down. we are open source and can be self-hosted so, you don't need to send your traces to us. We support existing `gen_ai` spec and ingestion over OTLP so, you can add this as a new exporter to your existing setup. We have a cloud version, you can quickly try the features with a $10 credit. We are looking to build more classifiers and enable people to build custom classifiers for their needs and would love to hear feedback on common failure modes people have built solutions or evaluation for Repo: https://github.com/tessaryai/tessary Website: https://tessary.ai Try for free: https://app.tessary.ai

projects.title: Show HN: Etchv – API for invisible watermarks in images, PDFs and videos
projects.author: agurha
projects.summary: Hello HN! The inspiration for Etchv came directly from friends who raised concerns about the growing ease of unauthorized media copying without attribution. To address this, Etchv embeds an invisible watermark inside images, PDFs, or short videos that survives modifications like screenshots, format changes, and file compression. You can try it on our homepage without signing up. There's also a live demo where a watermarked PDF page gets screenshotted and the watermark ID is still successfully recovered: https://etchv.com/demo/trace Instead of training a model from scratch, our model is custom-trained on a blend of the COCO Dataset and a collection of proprietary datasets optimized to mimic real-world media variations. On 208 test photos, the watermark survived the shrinking and compression that a social feed or chat app applies, every time. Tiny thumbnails mostly killed it—only 16 of 208 survived. Full benchmark results can be found here: https://etchv.com/solutions/creative-delivery#survival Limits: video is restricted to short clips for now (a few seconds at 360p), and PDFs max out at 8 pages. Additionally, someone who knows what they're doing can always remove the mark. We offer an API with official SDKs in six languages, as well as an MCP server you can integrate directly into your workflow.

projects.title: 开源了 12 个电商短视频 Agent Skills：一张商品图 → 带配音字幕的 15 秒竖屏视频，本地 ffmpeg 出片
projects.author: boisy
projects.summary: 之前发过一个电商出图的 Skills ，有人问能不能接着把图变成视频。这周把这部分也做完了，开源（ MIT ）： https://github.com/xianyu110/ecommerce-video-skills?utm_source=v2ex&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=ecommerce-video-skills&utm_content=body **想解决的问题**：让大模型写带货分镜很容易，但写完还得自己开剪映一镜一镜拖。我想让 agent 不光写脚本，还能把片子真剪出来。 **做法**：让 agent 输出一份 storyboard.json （每镜：用哪张图、怎么动、说什么、字幕高亮哪个词），然后本地一条命令渲染： ``` python scripts/assemble.py storyboard.json -o out/demo.mp4 ``` 脚本做的事：edge-tts 逐句配音 → 镜头时长按配音实际长度反推 → 静图做 Ken Burns （逐帧 scale+crop ，比 zoompan 稳）→ xfade 转场（居中在镜头分界，不吃配音）→ ASS 字幕 / 花字 / CTA → 合成一段免版权 BGM ，有人声时自动压低 → 两遍 loudnorm 到约 -14 LUFS → MP4 + SRT 。纯 Python + ffmpeg ，剪辑这一步不需要任何 API Key （ edge-tts 需要联网）。 **效果**：下面这条只用了一张 800×800 的随手拍，14.5 秒、1080×1920 ，我机器上 27 秒左右渲染完： ![]( https://upload.maynor1024.live/file/1791169828136_evs-one-photo-to-video.jpg) MP4： https://upload.maynor1024.live/file/1791169831745_evs-one-photo-demo-9x16.mp4 **拆成了 12 个 skill**，每个文件夹一个 SKILL.md ，可以只装需要的： - 3 秒钩子（ 9 种类型，≤18 字，带广告法禁用词自检） - 卖点分镜（ 15/30/60 秒结构，直接输出 storyboard.json ） - 图生视频提示词 / 多模型适配（ Seedance 、可灵、Veo 、Runway 、海螺、万相…，带商品一致性锁，不编造模型参数） - edge-tts 配音、字幕花字、ffmpeg 自动成片 - 平台导出（抖音 / TikTok Shop / 视频号 / 小红书 3:4 / 淘宝主图 1:1 / Amazon 16:9 ）+ 安全区预览 - 直播录像切 9:16 高光、开箱 / 对比评测模板、多语言配音（--lang en ）、封面标题 A/B **安装**：`npx skills add xianyu110/ecommerce-video-skills`，或者 Claude Code 里 `/plugin marketplace add xianyu110/ecommerce-video-skills`，或者直接把 skills/ 复制到 ~/.claude/skills / ~/.codex/skills / .cursor/skills 。不用 agent 的话，脚本也能单独跑，仓库里带了一个 6 张图的示例。 **已知局限**： - 静图 Ken Burns 终究不是实拍，适合测款和铺量，跑出数据的品建议补实拍； - 平台的时长 / 大小上限变化太快，没写死，导出时只给提示； - 示例商品是 AI 生成的虚构商品。 欢迎拍砖，尤其是做电商的朋友：哪些平台规格 / 模板最想要？

projects.title: 受 Jev 启发，花了三周、600 美元、20 多轮训了两个小模型专门做 Computer use
projects.author: gxcsoccer
projects.summary: 这三周业余时间做了个东西，开源出来给大家看看。 DeskMind 得心：一个在 Mac 上替你操作电脑的 agent ，决定每一步怎么做的是两个跑在本机的小模型（ Qwen3.5 0.8B 和 4B 微调，MLX ）。不走云端，也不按次付费。 思路来自 Jev：把每一步变成选择题，让模型给每个选项打分，而不是生成一段文字。区别是 Jev 是云端服务，我想要一个全在本机跑的版本，所以自己在 Qwen3.5 上训了 0.8B 和 4B 两个小模型。决策服务用的是和 Jev 相同的 `POST /v1/systemone` 请求格式，已有的 harness 换个地址就能接到本机。和 TypeSafe 没有任何关系。 0.8B 有把握就直接做（大约 0.5 秒），没把握就交给 4B 再判断（约 3.6 秒）。任务有两种理解的时候，它会先问你，比如表里有两笔 Lisa Wong 的订单，它会问你用哪一笔，而不是随便挑一个写进去。 ![]( https://raw.githubusercontent.com/deskmind-ai/deskmind/main/docs/images/asks-first.gif) 自己出了 13 个真机任务，每个跑 3 次，目前发布版是 38/39 ，没出现过没做完就说「完成」的情况。题是我自己出的、样本也小，仅供参考，逐题结果都公开了。 踩过最有意思的坑：标签平滑设成 0.95 ，结果 0.8B 的把握全挤在 0.96 这个门槛附近，七成的步骤都被交给了 4B ，所以现在速度还不够快。下一轮准备改。 目前的不足：「帮我整理这个文件夹」这种模糊的指令做得不好；文件很多的文件夹每步要几十秒；只支持 Apple 芯片，首次要下载约 5.3 GB 模型。 训练花了大约 600 美元：先在 Tinker 上跑，后来换阿里云 PAI ，最后按小时租显卡最划算。 - GitHub： https://github.com/deskmind-ai/deskmind - 下载 Mac App： https://deskmind.dev/zh/?ref=v2ex - 过程和踩坑： https://deskmind.dev/zh/blog/launch?ref=v2ex 欢迎下载试试，最想看到的是它该问却猜了的例子。

projects.title: Show HN: Spens sandboxed, observable coding agents
projects.author: floydhead01
projects.summary: Spens is a tool created to standardized sandboxing (good enough) and observability around coding agents. It leverages docker, nono and mitmproxy to create a reproducible sandbox environment for agents, that captures all traffic and helps you understand what your coding agent is doing and when. Right now pi, opencode, claude and codex are supported out of the box, with node and python - but you can configure any agent or environment. It was created under the realization while working under different repos and agents, that 1. agents do weird stuff sometimes (like try and nuke a folder or poke around your HD) 2. statistics and usage collection is not really consistent (and some like Claude and Codex try and hide info) 3. reproducibility of agents across devices was challenging. Instead of setting up bespoke environments each time , we needed a way to automate it. And thus Spens was born. One note on the security aspect - I write good enough cause it is docker so unless your running something like gVisor it is possible for the agent to escape the sandbox (esp with a loose nono config) - all though in practice I've not seen this behavior. projects.title: Show HN: Keel – Give your agent a typed strategy language, not a trading account
projects.author: zferland
projects.summary: I’ve been using AI agents to build systematic strategies on Hyperliquid for over a year, and slowly built up a reliable system to represent, test and deploy strategies. Typically there are a few options 1) llm in the execution loop, ie it makes decisions and trades, but that is slow, inconsistent and hard to audit 2) you have an agent write all the code, backtest etc, but it makes tons of subtle mistakes with time series data and diff timeframe etc, and is often not reusing bits. There are some ways to improve this of course with right frameworks and setups. But its still hard to be confident in its correctness and its hard for you to verify quickly. With Keel we built a small typed language (DSL) to represent strategies. It uses a well defined set of components to build a DAG of steps, it carries types and clocks. This allows agents to build these strategies with a really fast feedback loop as they can be quickly validated and many common errors avoided. In a DAG its also easy to inspect intermediate results. Valid strategies are fingerprinted and the exact same artifact runs in backtesting and live. These strategies are also much easier for humans to verify as they are self describing components, and mostly linear to read and reason about. Still trying to improve the space of how many types of different strategies can be represented in this and still trying to improve how well LLMs go from natural language to strategy. A lot of the improvements come from just giving the agents better and faster tools and faster feedback loops.

It grew considerably beyond that original idea. Yengi is a .NET 10 / WPF desktop application with: * Agent and tool system for files, terminal, Git, builds and tests * RAG and LSP integration * Verification loops with checkpoints and rollback * 30+ agent tools * Support for local models and external APIs * A custom 1.5B router model that I fine-tuned on thousands of examples of Yengi-specific agent decisions * 200+ automated tests It also has three additional modes besides the coding environment: *Blender:* Yengi can communicate with Blender, generate `bpy` scripts, keep conversational scene context, and optionally inspect Blender viewport screenshots through a multimodal model. I also added an optional prompt-engineering layer. For example, "create a low-poly tree" is expanded into a more detailed 3D-oriented instruction before being sent to the model. A follow-up such as "add five red apples to this tree" can modify the existing scene rather than starting from scratch. *Unity:* Yengi can work with Unity projects, generate C# components and interact with the Unity Editor. *Image generation:* Images can be generated from the development environment and saved directly into the project. The unusual part is how I built it. I used AI coding tools heavily, particularly Google Antigravity and GitHub Copilot. I didn't manually type the majority of the C# code. My role was primarily architecture, agent behavior, security boundaries, verification and rollback logic, router training, testing, debugging AI-generated changes, and integrating the different systems. I'm still trying to figure out how much of this approach is genuinely useful and how much is me having fun building increasingly complicated things. The project is free and open source under AGPL-3.0: https://github.com/mdaiWorks/yengi I'd especially like feedback from people working with .NET/C#, coding agents, local models, Blender or Unity. In particular, I'm curious about: * Is a small fine-tuned local router actually useful for this kind of agent? * Does the verification/rollback architecture make sense? * Are the Blender/Unity integrations useful beyond being demos? * If you were building this, what would you simplify or change? projects.title: Show HN: OpenAPPA – open-source deterministic guardrails that don't break agents
projects.author: motakuk
projects.summary: Hi Hacker News! Matvey, one of the authors, is here. While building enterprise agents, we ran into a problem: the more tools you connect to the AI, the higher the chance it will run out of control and leak sensitive data. Guardrails, in theory, should prevent this, but the situation is worrying: - Non-deterministic guardrails (LLM as a judge, auto modes, etc.) are vulnerable to prompt injections, or they lack knowledge of the data, making them inefficient (~10% data leaks on our benchmarks). - Existing deterministic guardrails (Cedar, OPA, FIDES, Dogwood) require massive case-specific IF-ELSE-like policies and break agents (~59% utility loss on our benchmarks). We did something differently. We’ve taken the best of existing deterministic guardrails and built a policy language that is data-specific, not use-case specific. It lets you scale agents without updating a policy. On top of that, we’ve added multiple tricks (like a remedy plan or a DualLLM pattern) to help agents operate within those restrictions, raising utility from ~40% to ~90% and making it the first deterministic guardrail that doesn't break agents. Finally, we’ve designed it to be pluggable into any agent loop with pre- and post-tool-call hooks. We invite you to check out our benchmarks: https://www.openappa.com/evaluation Play with it in Claude Code: https://www.openappa.com/claude-code Try plugging it into your agent: https://www.openappa.com/add-to-agent Or check the academic paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24625 We'd love to hear any feedback!

projects.title: Show HN: I emulated Roborock's cloud so my vacuum works without internet
projects.author: Lash-L
projects.summary: Hi! I maintain the python-roborock library and the Roborock integration in Home Assistant. Roborock vacuums use a local protocol for direct commands, but they still route all map data strictly through the cloud (even though the map is stored locally). Even worse, if you try to block the vacuum from accessing the internet on your router, it will constantly reboot its Wi-Fi connection trying to re-establish a cloud connection, meaning you can't rely on just using a private local connection. I built a self-hostable version of Roborock's cloud: https://github.com/Python-roborock/local_roborock_server It works without having to open the device or root it, taking advantage of a couple of quirks during the onboarding process: 1) The vacuum has api-%s.roborock.com baked into its firmware. It injects the region directly into the string and this is the first exploit we take advantage of. The app will send in your region as a two letter code, e.g. 'us', 'eu', 'cn'. We send in a full URL ending with a '/' (e.g. 'example.com/'). The vacuum then treats "api-example.com" as the host and the rest as the URL path(e.g. 'api-example.com/.roborock.com'), directing its traffic to your server so long as there is a valid HTTPS certificate on that domain. 2) The second part of the handshake requires encrypting a message via a public key that is stored on Roborock's cloud where the private key pair is on the vacuum. We are able to reverse engineer the public key as the robot sends signatures with its message. Because of how RSA works, each signature is mathematically tied to the secret public key plus some extra noise. By gathering a few signatures across multiple onboarding attempts and taking their greatest common divisor, the noise cancels out and cleanly isolates the vacuum's actual public key which allows the server to encrypt its response and complete the pairing. I have a full technical write up here: https://python-roborock.github.io/local_roborock_server/tech... I wanted to share this on HN as I think this points to a very interesting thing that is happening. I have been playing with this idea for years in my head and I have not been able to get it to work (and I am not the only one who had looked into the api-%s avenue). I'm not a cryptography expert and had no idea that the signature exploit was even possible. I was stuck for long enough that I decided to throw the problem at some long-running agents, and they found the greatest common divisor exploit. IoT companies put most of their security effort into the cloud, since that's what they actually run. The vacuum is just one device on someone's home network, so it gets less attention and corners get cut. I think LLMs that are willing to throw themselves at a problem for hours are going to make stuff like this a lot easier to pull off and a lot more common.

projects.summary: 大家好，我是 WebDecoy 的 Chris Portscheller，FCaptcha 的开发团队成员。这是一次项目自荐。 FCaptcha 是一个采用 MIT 许可证、可自行部署的开源 CAPTCHA 项目，提供复选框和无感模式，不使用图片或音频谜题。它结合浏览器信号、交互行为与工作量证明（Proof of Work），用于辅助识别自动化访问。 提供 Go、Node.js 和 Python 服务端实现。 提供公开 Docker 镜像 ghcr.io/webdecoy/fcaptcha，支持 Linux AMD64 / ARM64；自行部署无需注册托管服务账号。 最近补充了 Docker 部署指南，以及可直接运行的 Node.js 联系表单示例。示例包含浏览器端获取令牌、后端验证、hostname/action 校验、令牌重放拒绝和验证服务故障处理。 表单示例使用 Node.js 22+，支持日语/英语切换，仅用于本地演示，不发送邮件或保存消息。

projects.summary: 自荐一个最近做的开源项目 GitScry - 你的git历史就是一座藏宝库。 GitScry 是一个用 Rust 编写的命令行工具。它希望解决一个问题：很多对开发很有价值的信息，其实已经存在于 Git 历史里，但通常需要手动组合 git log、git blame、旧 diff、revert 记录和文件历史才能找到。 GitScry 会把这些历史整理成可以直接查询的问题，例如： 以前有没有实现过类似的改动？ 某一行代码或某个 symbol 为什么会存在？ 哪些文件历史上经常一起修改？ 修改这个文件时，通常还需要看哪些测试？ 某种方案以前是否尝试过，后来又被放弃或 revert？ 哪个 commit 可能引入了当前 regression？ 已知一个 bug fix，最初引入这段错误代码的是哪个改动？ 一些特点 完全基于本地 Git history，Git 仍然是 source of truth 本地建立可重建缓存，不需要上传代码，你的藏宝库永远属于你自己 查询结果会保留对应的 commit、path、confidence 和 evidence 支持 Linux、macOS 和 Windows 人类与 agent 均可以使用 目前已经在 git/git、curl/curl、rust-lang/rust、NousResearch/hermes-agent 等真实仓库历史上测试过不同查询，README 里放了一些 benchmark 和实际示例。 项目目前还在早期阶段，欢迎使用和反馈。

projects.title: [开源推荐] greencheck：用变异测试查你的质量门禁是不是摆设
projects.author: simin-yuan

github.description: Your checks are green because they never ran. Audit the instruments an agent uses to report on itself.

projects.summary: 很多项目 CI 一路全绿，不是因为代码没问题，而是那条检查规则从来没真正生效过。greencheck 会在你的配置和代码里自动制造小改动：删掉一行、把数值改成 0、清空一个字段，然后看你的门禁还拦不拦得住。拦不住的地方，就是它根本没在管的地方。纯 Python 标准库实现，零第三方依赖，装完直接用，不用改你现有的门禁配置。 亮点 1. 审计的对象是「门禁本身」而不是被检查的代码。同类工具大多在查代码，查检查规则的很少。 2. 零依赖、pip install 完就能跑，也可以直接 python -m greencheck.cli 调用，不侵入现有 CI。 3. 示例自带、可复现：仓库里的 demo 会当场跑出一个逃逸的变异——把 "replicas": 3 改成 0（一个永远起不来的服务），而门禁只说「键都在、值都非空」，所以放行。结构上的每条规则都还成立，这正是这类缺口能活下来的原因。 4. 不夸大：输出明确写着「这些是值得你去想的问题，不是结论」，不会拿变异数冒充缺陷数。 5. 同一个思路还能用来审计指标：一个永远等于 1.0 的自评分，不是测量出来的，是装饰。

projects.title: [开源推荐] precheck：让你的 AI agent 用「它无权编写」的检查自证
projects.author: simin-yuan

github.name: simin-yuan/precheck
github.description: Make an agent prove its claims with checks it was not allowed to write. The check is frozen before the run, then audited for the ability to fail at all.

projects.summary: AI agent 说它做完了，你现在只有两个选择：信它，或者自己把 diff 重看一遍。precheck 给第三个选项。它做两件测试框架不会做的事：第一，验收检查必须在动工之前写好并被哈希锁死，所以干活的那一方没法把考试题目改成自己会的；事后改一个字，之前所有结论全部作废——这是可验证的，不是靠约定。第二，检查通过之后，它会把被检查的产物改坏再跑一遍；在坏输入上照样通过的检查，从来就不是证据。 亮点 1. 审计的对象是「证明本身」。pytest 问的是「代码对不对」，precheck 问的是「你的证明对不对」——后者目前几乎没有工具。 2. 预注册是机制不是口号：检查在开工前冻结入哈希链，precheck verify 一条命令就能查出事后改动、删条目、跳序号。任何人拿到仓库都能自己验，不需要信任你。 3. 变异审计带具体改动：4 种变异（删行 / 置空 / 改数 / 截断）确定性地改坏产物再跑，逃逸的检查逐条列出改成了什么，比如 replicas: 3 -> 0 —— 一个永远起不来的服务，检查照样说通过。 4. 零依赖纯标准库、不联网、不侵入现有 CI；19 个单测；Linux / Windows / macOS × Python 3.8–3.13 全绿（9/9）。自带 composite GitHub Action。 5. 不夸大：输出明确写着「这是问题列表，不是 bug 列表」，README 有独立的 Limits 段落讲清它证明不了什么——包括「哈希链只能证明历史没被事后改动，不能证明第一条记录是诚实的」。

projects.summary: Hi, as I kept getting confused by having multiple Claude sessions open, last weekend I decided to combine two of my favorite emerging technologies and give it a try: Software Factory and JEV. The idea is simple, inspired by GitHub Actions, I wanted a way to "queue" agent work on my local laptop, with the ability to define different pipelines via YAML. Each pipeline runs in its own Git worktree, so it's isolated from the others. I'm using some pipelines: dev: code → test → commit plan: plan → human review → code → test → commit security: code → human review → test → security review → commit frontend: code → React test → build → commit A request can move up and down the pipeline and be reworked if an agent or JEV flags it! I'm also using JEV to check if a potential secret is leaked, if the coding agent output asks for human review, etc. The real magic happens when you take a single Agent session as the main driver. You can then plan and queue multiple features at once. I think it worked out pretty well, so I open sourced it: https://github.com/stratonext/software-factory You can try it yourself with: uv tool install software-factory Note: You need a JEV key if you want to use the judging steps.

projects.title: Show HN: Ox – A local agent that uses the internet for you
projects.author: ziyzhu
projects.summary: I’ve been building Ox, a local, open-source agent that uses the internet for you. Ox acts as an intelligent proxy between you and the internet. It uses websites and apps on your behalf, freeing you from attention-hungry interfaces and slow legacy services. As it works, it can turn what it learns into reusable actions (basically function calls), making future interactions deterministic and way faster. Most service integrations today are still built ahead of time: someone writes an API integration, connector, MCP server, or browser automation and then maintains it as the service changes. But the internet is becoming more dynamic so have our agents. With Ox, instead of waiting for a connector, you can say something like: “Connect to <service>.” Ox can study a website or workflow through capabilities it already has, turn what it learns into typed actions and reusable skills, validate them, and make them available immediately. That pushed me toward local agents. A local agent operates from your own device, network, and existing authenticated browser sessions instead of relying on shared datacenter infrastructure. This also makes it less likely to hit blocks aimed at datacenter IPs or centralized browser automation. The model doesn’t need your passwords, cookies, or session tokens. Authentication and browser state are owned by the Host, while the agent interacts through explicit actions that could be gated. Ox is completely free and open source. You can use any model provider, including local or self-hosted models, while keeping your agent’s data on device. As local models improve, I think this architecture becomes increasingly useful because the agent can become more capable without requiring more of your data to leave your device. The security model is also a big part of the design. Ox asks before taking sensitive actions, keeps credentials isolated from the model, limits what agent code can access, and lets you stop execution at any time. Underneath the app is OpenOx, an open protocol for self-evolving agents. It separates the interface, agent, model provider, persistent state, execution environment, and external capabilities. The agent can run JavaScript inside a capability-limited VM. The VM has no direct network access, Host filesystem access, shell, Node.js, or DOM. Anything outside the VM has to go through an explicit ox.* capability exposed by the Host. Services provide typed actions for websites, device capabilities, or MCP servers. Skills provide reusable instructions for combining those actions. New services and skills can be attached at runtime without waiting for a new version of the app. They can remain local or be recorded in Git and shared through repositories, so each Ox can evolve independently while benefiting from capabilities learned by others. The agent’s persistent state lives in a portable Ox Profile containing its identity, memory, skills, artifacts, and conversations. The goal is for that state to stay independent of any particular interface, including Ox itself, or model provider. File over app. The first implementation is an iOS app. It’s available on the App Store, and the whole thing is open source: https://openox.ai/ https://github.com/ziyzhu/openox If you’re interested in the broader motivation behind the project, I wrote about it here: https://ziyzhu.com/a-technology-for-free-will This is still early. I’m especially interested in feedback on the security model and self-evolution. I built Ox from scratch but many aspects of the project were heavily inspired by Pi/OpenClaw and the idea of malleable software. Ox’s core agent loop on iOS is pretty much a Swift rewrite of the Pi core package. Happy to answer anything about the implementation or protocol.

projects.title: Show HN: HookDeploy – Webhook infra with mTLS private delivery
projects.author: mbernstein01
projects.summary: Hi HN! I'm Michael and I built HookDeploy. HookDeploy is a webhook infrastructure tool that captures webhooks at the edge, allows for inspection, transformation and fanout to multiple destinations including to your own private infrastructure with our first-party (source-available) mTLS agent. Runs as a service on Linux, lives in the tray on Windows and in the menu bar on Mac. As I'm sure most of you you have felt webhooks kind of suck if things don't go exactly as planned. Dropped webhooks or failures are likely silent. What actually drove me to build this was cleaning up after major cloud outages more than once. Cross referencing what System A knew against what System B actually had and reentering data by hand or trying to simulate events firing again. I have spent weeks of my life cleaning up webhook failures. HookDeploy solves that problem with a button and intelligent grouping of failed requests into incidents. If you've ever seen or had to clean up after a ransomware attack - you understand why I'd prefer to keep my firewall as tight as possible too. Our agent enables developers and teams to keep ports closed - if there is nothing to scan, there is nothing to attack. Getting to our own mTLS agent was a journey of trying to integrate existing solutions: first WireGuard (too much operational overhead), then Tailscale which was excellent, but it had real drawbacks on the required memory per joined tailnet and the additional cost to a user's Tailscale bill. It took several months to get it right, but it was worth every week of it. A few things to note at launch: we are launching with security measures in place: data is encrypted at rest with org-scoped keys rotated weekly (BYOK is on the roadmap), segregated databases for US, EU, APAC and AU so customer data stays where customers are not traversing underwater fiber to come to the US. We have 7 private delivery exit regions: San Francisco (us-west), New York (us-east), London (uk-london), Amsterdam (eu-west), Frankfurt (eu-central), Singapore (ap-southeast) and Sydney (au-southeast). Our platform is built primarily on Cloudflare for speed and security utilizing workers, KV, R2, Queues, Tunnels/VPC, and of course DNS and security. This has been some time in the making and I am excited to answer your questions and get feedback! Thank you in advance!

projects.title: Show HN: AI·rete·RAG – a Rete rule engine decides, RAG explains why
projects.author: ZaharaHussain
projects.summary: Hi HN, I built ai·rete·rag because I kept seeing teams put an LLM in charge of decisions that need to be auditable (lending, fraud, clinical triage), then bolt on "guardrails" after the fact. It runs the two in series instead: 1. A pure-Python Rete engine evaluates YAML rules against your facts. The verdict comes only from here. Same facts, same verdict, every time, with salience-based conflict resolution. 2. RAG retrieves passages from your own policy documents, and an LLM writes a plain-English explanation of the decision that was already made, citing those passages. It can't change the verdict. A few things that went further than I expected: - Rules are a graph, not flat lists: nested all/any/not, and rules can assert facts that other rules consume (forward chaining). The decision trace shows the causal chain. - Audit mode records every rule evaluated, including the ones that didn't fire, condition by condition, with a snapshot of the rule set for replay. - Rules can steer retrieval (a fired rule narrows which documents get searched), and retrieved text can be turned into facts for the engine. - Non-technical authors can build rules in a visual editor, or paste a policy document and get LLM-drafted rules with citations. Drafts are never saved without review. YAML is still there for engineers. The landing page has a live demo with no signup (8 demo domains: loan, fraud, clinical, insurance, legal, ops, e-commerce, blockchain). There's also an MCP server, so Claude and other agents can call /decide as a tool: `uvx ai-rete-rag-mcp`. To be upfront: it's a hosted product with a free tier. The MCP client is open source (MIT, github.com/zaharajabeen13-create/ai-rete-rag-mcp); the engine and platform are not open source right now. I'd especially like to hear from anyone who has had to explain an automated decision to a regulator or an auditor: what did they actually ask for?

projects.title: Show HN: ScopeTrail – audit receipts for multi-hop agent delegation
projects.author: mrjimmy1
projects.summary: With the growth of the agentic economy and the ability of agents to manage wallets and make payments it's critical that we have a mechanism to audit their payment behavior. And to complicate matters, agents are invoking subagents to work faster. When an agent hands work to another agent, OAuth Token Exchange (RFC 8693) nests an "act" claim at each hop. Those claims are informational, not enforceable. Each actor in the process (e.g., your identity manager, your gateway, each agent) logged its activity — and no artifact anywhere answers "did this action, three steps from the user, stay inside what the user actually authorized?" Cloudflare (Wallets, and Cloudflare OS's Gatekeepers) enforces scope at call time against its own ledger, and Block's Buzz mints an owner→agent authorization a third party can verify offline without calling Block — ScopeTrail is the layer above both, proving scope actually attenuated across every hop and returning a verdict on the action at the end. ScopeTrail is a TypeScript library (Apache 2.0) that lives above the multi-agent transaction and documents the full chain by: - Building and validating the chain from raw tokens - Minting and signing a receipt with Ed25519 over JCS (RFC 8785), and - Storing the receipt in an AT Protocol PDS. The user can then retrieve and verify the receipt including the hop and scope if the agents went beyond their remit. Raw tokens are never stored — only SHA-256 digests. Verification is stateless: no callback to the issuer is needed at verify time, no vendor in the loop. You can try it now! Verify a live receipt by: curl -sO https://scopetrail.github.io/.well-known/jwks.json npx -y --package=@scopetrail/core view-receipt \ at://did:plc:bty3gmskhla7rwblq5zl5jm5/dev.scopetrail.auditReceipt/00MSQDN0UT747ADDB2C4BB25420974 \ --jwks jwks.json This view-receipt call resolves the DID, fetches the receipt, checks its Ed25519 signature against the JWKS downloaded before the call, and prints the delegation chain. The next milestone will be mint-by-default inside an open-source MCP gateway. If you work on gateways, an agent platform, or an identity product, I'd like to hear where this breaks.

projects.title: Show HN: DrivingBench – Frontier LLMs Driving a Real Toyota Corolla
projects.author: aditya-ramabadr
projects.summary: Hi all, wanted to share a cool project me and two buddies have been working on. Essentially we took a Toyota Corolla, installed a Comma 4, hooked it up to GPT-6 Astra/Claude Fable/Grok 4.6/Sol, gave them MCP tools to control the Toyota, and then we let them try driving a cone course (in an empty parking lot at low speed). They can observe the cameras/telemetry, request steering/speed, and stop the car. The goal was to see how good frontier LLMs might be just out-of-the-box at a task like driving a real physical car (inspired by recent such demos in robotics). The best model was GPT-6 Astra which fully finished the course on its second attempt (which was pretty shocking to us). We gave each model up to 3 attempts on the course in the same chat conversation (to incentivize in-context learning). Fable also improved quite a bit from 9% to 45% by its 3rd attempt. We also have a trace viewer at our website (for example see https://drivingbench.com/trace/gpt-6-astra/2/ for Astra's successful attempt), and everything is open source (traces, harness/code at https://github.com/aditya-ramabadran/drivingbench_harness_v1 , we have a report at https://drivingbench.com/report/ on how we did everything, some of the things that went wrong or that we could do better, etc). Obvious disclaimer: the models clearly aren't good enough to drive on an actual road yet. Also we did this at super low speeds in an open parking lot with a human always ready to brake at any time. Please use the harness/code/etc at your own risk. Would love to answer any questions or take any feedback for v2!

projects.title: Show HN: MCPJam - the first testing & evaluations platform for MCP servers
projects.author: prathmeshmcp
projects.summary: Prathmesh, CEO of MCPJam here. Users now start in ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and other AI clients. They reach your product through your MCP server. That means your users often aren’t in your product anymore. You can’t see what they prompted for, how the agent interpreted it, or whether your server helped them get the result they wanted. I saw this firsthand leading MCP technical strategy at Asana, including our ChatGPT and Claude launches. We were building high-stakes enterprise integrations, but we had no reliable way to test them the way we test normal software- or to know whether they worked once they reached real users. I started using MCPJam for those problems after re-connecting with my former coworker who created the project. brought it to more of our developers, and worked it into our CI/CD pipeline. I joined the team because I kept hearing the same issue from other companies building for agents. So, what does “good” look like for MCP? For us, it means users reliably get the outcome they came for, across the AI clients they use. That’s what we’ve been building toward. MCPJam now helps you test the full workflow, from the first prompt to the expected result: * Swarms: Simulate users with different goals and prompts to find where workflows break across AI clients. * User Testing: Watch how real users interact with your MCP product, where they get stuck, and how they feel about the results. * Evals: Turn those workflows into repeatable tests that check whether users get the expected outcome. * CI/CD: Run those evals across AI clients before each release to catch regressions. Over 106,000 developers and +300 enterprises use our open-source solution to see how their servers behave locally across major AI clients. MCPJam has grown from a debugging tool into a continuous testing and evaluation workflow for MCP servers. If you’re building an MCP server or agent-facing product, give MCPJam a try. What is the hardest thing for you to test? We love hearing about your MCP server builds!

projects.title: Show HN: Linting 216 public Claude Code skills – 69% won't reliably trigger
projects.author: sgharlow
projects.summary: I built a linter for Claude Code artifacts (skills, subagents, slash commands, .mcp.json configs, and plugins) and then pointed it at a pile of public repos to see what people actually ship. A few of the numbers surprised me enough that I wrote them up. The one that stuck: across 87 public subagents, 57% (50 of 87) declare no `tools` list at all. That reads like a safe default, but it's the opposite. A subagent with no `tools` inherits the caller's entire toolbox, Bash included. Permission prompts still gate execution, but a worker you meant to "just read code" now carries the grant surface to run shell — the opposite of least-privilege. Add 16 more that grant bare `Bash` and 8 that grant a wildcard, and 85% of the sample isn't least-privilege. Other findings from the two scans: - Of 215 public skills scored for triggering, 69% have a `description` that won't reliably trigger (40% outright unlikely to fire, 28% borderline). "My skill never fires" is the #1 real-world failure, and it hides in one frontmatter line. - 83% of subagents (72 of 87) lack invocation cues ("use when…") in their description. - 1 of 216 skills, and 0 of 87 subagents, pass every check cleanly. Almost everyone got secrets right: only 6 of 216 skills tripped the scanner. How it works: mostly pure, deterministic checks that emit file:line evidence ("SKILL.md:14 links ./references/converter.md, not found"). An optional LLM check (bring your own key) judges whether a description will actually trigger. The CLI is free (`npx skillcrossroads ./my-skill`), there's a GitHub Action that gates PRs, and it's open-core: the public audits are free, money is a hosted Pro tier. Limits: the two reports ran different editions (skills on rubric v1.2 with the LLM checks, agents on v1.2 deterministic-only), both labeled, tree SHAs pinned, reproduction commands published. The rubric is strict on purpose, and every finding carries file:line evidence you can check against the artifact itself. The sample is 216 skills across 18 repos and 123 agents/commands (87 subagents + 36 commands) across 10 repos, caps disclosed, and you can re-run it on your own repos. Reports: https://skillcrossroads.com/report?ref=hn-show and https://skillcrossroads.com/report-agents?ref=hn-show Code: https://github.com/sgharlow/skillcrossroads

projects.title: Show HN: Ax-check.com – Can agents use your product?
projects.author: 0x63_Problems
projects.summary: I'm the co-founder of Gauge, and I built ax-check.com to quickly test how well coding agents can onboard to your product. You'll get a scorecard, specific suggested fixes, and three full coding sessions that show how agents read your site and use your product. I built this because similar checks were too noisy. Most suggested obscure technical changes that don't actually make a difference in agent experience (or AX, hence ax-check.com). This check starts by using DeepSeek 4.1 Flash to try to find key information about your product, starting from the homepage. In actual agent traffic data, we've seen that the key pages are the homepage, llms.txt, pricing, and the docs site (by traffic volume, and by influence), so we focus on those and ignore the rest. We also find that content negotiation for Markdown is legitimately helpful for agents to complete tasks faster and find what they're looking for, so the scan tests that your key pages can serve Markdown. The other key piece is that we run actual coding agents in sandboxes, and have them try to onboard to your product. You can see the full trace and watch it happen live (we kick it off fresh when you enter a new site). We surface interesting findings like hallucinated URLs, inaccurate docs instructions, or product confusion. It also detects whether the agents could complete a fully working onboarding autonomously, without being blocked by a login wall. This is still controversial, but I think finding ways to let agents safely onboard autonomously is going to be table stakes within a year for developer tools in particular. The whole site is agent-friendly itself! You can generally just talk to your coding agent about ax-check.com and it can do the rest. Would really appreciate any feedback to make this useful.

projects.title: Show HN: Droid ASC – An On-Demand Android Decompiler, 41–269x Faster Than JADX
projects.author: mgaldys4
projects.summary: A few days ago, I was using JADX MCP to analyze my phone, but JADX MCP was just too laggy. I had a large number of APKs to analyze, and nearly every one of them required spinning up a new JADX process. With just two or three of them, my computer ran out of memory. The efficiency was terribly low, so I came up with an idea and wrote a script. I built a on-demand Android decompiler called Droid ASC. Literally dozens to hundreds of times faster than JADX, no exaggeration. Here are the benchmark charts. I tested APKs across 4 orders of magnitude. For a ~50MB APK, a global cross reference index search takes 400ms, which is 41 times faster than JADX. For a 300MB APK, it takes only 1.79s, which is 269 times faster than JADX. I have stopped using jadx mcp entirely. ASC can analyze dozens of APKs in parallel with no problem. Here is an experiment I ran: using GPT5.6 + ASC, with almost no human intervention, an automated pipeline ran for two days straight. It analyzed every APK with uid=1000 on my device, pulling in nearly 100 APK/JAR/APEX files. In the end it found one RCE vuln, one system uid arbitrary file write vuln, two vulnerabilities that can execute ROOT commands, and one SELinux restricted vulnerability that can execute ROOT commands. Pretty wild!

projects.title: Show HN: Pinocchio: Harness for Verifiable Work
projects.author: lazaruslong
projects.summary: Hey HN, we've been trying to solve LLM Hallucinations. So we built Pinocchio. Pinocchio is a research preview for AI outputs with provenance and verification built in. Give it a task and source material. For numerics, the values used in the computation are carried directly from the source rather than regenerated by the model across reasoning steps. Pinocchio records the computations and derivations applied to them, and a deterministic verifier can replay and check the resulting computation. The output retains a connection to: • the exact source inputs used • the operations performed on them • the intermediate and final results they produced • the checks those results passed Every output points back to its sources. You can trace it backwards through its derivation and sources. Really looking forward to what you guys think about this. P.S. we're limiting to one run at a time. Other than there are no other restrictions. It does take a while though, so I'd let it be and check back in a while.

projects.author: b4timer
projects.summary: Hey HN, Adam here. We built a small MCP example around a single problem: How do you let an agent use a tool that needs credentials without giving the credentials to the agent? The demo has two tools. One is open. One is protected. When the agent calls the protected tool, Keydris checks the policy first: ALLOW → run the tool REJECT → stop The credential stays on the server. The agent never sees it. We do the check through a small middleware on the MCP server called the KIT Reader. Repo: https://github.com/keydrisLabs/mcp-auth-keydris-template We're early. If you're building with MCP, Claude Code or Codex, I'd love to know how you're handling this today and where you think this approach breaks. We support other elements like integrations etc but would love your feedback

projects.title: Show HN: ClientCoded – QA Platform for AI Agents
projects.author: travishcronin
projects.summary: Hi HN. We built a QA platform for AI agents. My cofounder spent 6 years at Veeva Systems building QA frameworks for regulated software. I spent 5 years in sales helping AI-native startups with their growth. We've both seen the issues companies face when deploying agents without a structured way of testing and monitoring them. The engineering teams we interviewed prior to building said they are doing manual spot-checks or just using LLM as a judge to check discrepancies. We generate synthetic test environments for 35 platforms (Salesforce, Jira, Stripe, Zendesk, Datadog, and 29 more). Each environment has ~200 adversarial queries with computed ground truth across 7 categories: clean lookups, ambiguous questions, multi-step operations, scope boundary tests, contradictory inputs, invalid assumptions, and context-dependent questions. The ground truth is initially computed by running SQL against the synthetic dataset so it's not just guessed by an LLM. We also do adversarial testing for pre-production conversational agents. The system generates different personas that push agents off-script and scores pass/fail across 10 dimensions so you can see what happens in realistic customer scenarios. Our production monitoring is just one webhook with every conversation evaluated in real time as well. We are two founders bootstrapping and we would love feedback on our approach! https://clientcoded.com/

projects.title: Show HN: Charter – Operate production-safe agents that run on your own infra
projects.author: alama24
projects.summary: Even though everyone is talking about AI agents doing everything for them at work, many companies still aren't using autonomous agents to automate real operational work internally. Usually it's because of the complexity of bootstrapping an agent from scratch that’s production-safe (won’t spend all your company’s budget, burn through compute costs because it runs too often, or call a tool that breaks a customer). Even with today's agent-building frameworks, running agents reliably in production often means stitching together LangChain, Temporal, observability tools, approval systems, and custom guardrail logic. And that’s just for running an agent safely: there also has to be a management system so someone can observe and operate all their agents (upgrade it, roll it back, stop it). We wanted to build the end-to-end internal agent infrastructure that every company has to build today to use production-safe agents internally as an open-source platform. The important thing is that getting an agent running safely is quick and simple: someone can first define their agent tying it to a version, and their lifecycle and runtime policies in YAML. Next they register their agents on workers in YAML and run those workers wherever they want. This means that if one AKS cluster has permissions for the tools needed for agents X and Y and another has permissions for agents A and B, they would each register those agents on their respective clusters. Finally they can use the CLI to apply and run the agent, and then manage it with approvals, responding to questions its asking, upgrade it/roll it back/pause it (via either CLI or a UI/portal running on localhost that are communicating with the control plane). Some of the agent lifecycle management can be automated by the system: metric-based lifecycle policies make it so a user can say “if this new agent version I’m trying out (with a different prompt) fails 10 times, roll it back to the old version” or “if the new agent version is spending over a certain amount in the last 5 runs block it from being run anymore till I debug and resume it”. This is useful for teams that want to run many agents without needing someone on standby to intervene if something goes wrong on any one of them. The control plane is self-hostable or can be run via a managed cloud offering, and the self-hostable option combined with someone doing local inference is actually a completely air-gapped system. Give it a try: https://github.com/boundflow/charter and let us know what you think.

projects.title: Show HN: Automatically keep track of all features implemented in a project
projects.author: krzysiek
projects.summary: I built this because I wanted to automate my least favourite part of documentation writing - expressing at a high level what was implemented. There are a couple of situations where you could need that: - to show to the client what changed since the last update - to show to an executive, where the fucus went lately - to explain to a new team member, what the project is about Because the report (you can see how it looks here: https://github.com/netizer/feature-ledger/blob/main/docs/cli... ) is automated, I also use it as a discovery tool in projects I just started working on. The way it works: - `ledger init` - creates a `.ledger` directory; descriptions of all new features will be stored there - `ledger bootstrap` - prints out a prompt to be used in a coding agent; it will analyse a new codebase and create the JSON files describing all features - `ledger audit` - when you usa a coding agent it will automatically keep the feature list up-to-date, audit is to discover features implemented without a coding agent - `ledger release cut --name "Release name" --date 2026-09-11` - run it after you've just shown to the client what had changed and you want to start working on a new set of features; in the new ledger you will see new features in green, updated features with blue, and deleted ones in red - `ledger build` - run it whenever you want to see the report of new features; there are 3 files generated based on JSON files describing features: a PDF for the client, FEATURES.md (the same but in an MD format), FEATURES_EXTENDED.md (the same but including implementation details - this is for the dev team)
